Diadem leaf-nosed bats demonstrate a relatively rapid early ontogeny, with neonates born at a wet weight of approximately 5.8 grams [Wwb = approximately 5.8 grams]. This modest birth mass, inferred from comparative data on the closely related Rhinolophus ferrumequinum, places the newborn at a distinct developmental disadvantage compared to larger-bodied congeners. Field observations of maternal behavior indicate that the suckling juvenile remains entirely dependent on milk for the first several weeks of life. The transition to nutritional independence occurs when the offspring reaches an age of 40 days after birth [tx = 40 days after birth], a milestone achieved when average roost temperatures hover near 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C]. This weaning age is relatively concise for an insectivorous bat of this body plan, suggesting that the local abundance of aerial prey allows mothers to provision their pup efficiently. The elevated metabolic demands of lactation are substantial, and a female must successfully balance the energetic costs of milk synthesis against her own maintenance before the young can begin capturing prey independently. The precise timing of weaning likely varies with local climatic conditions and insect availability.

Adult females of this species attain a maximum body mass of approximately 50 grams [Wwi = approximately 50 grams], with recorded field specimens ranging between 34 and 50 grams. This ultimate wet weight is reflective of a moderately sized hipposiderid that occupies a specialized niche hunting large beetles and moths within the forest understory. In captivity, females provided ad libitum access to mealworms and a controlled thermal environment at 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C] exhibited a peak resting metabolic rate of 33.00 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 33.00 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This measurement of maximal basal oxygen consumption underscores the species' relatively high metabolic throughput, which is necessary to sustain its active foraging strategy. Comparative data from other members of the family Hipposideridae suggest that this value is typical for bats of a similar mass that do not regularly enter deep torpor. The maintenance of such a metabolic rate imposes a constant demand for high-calorie insect prey, and during periods of scarcity, individuals may be forced to reduce activity or enter shallow daily torpor to conserve energy.

Reproductive output in the Diadem leaf-nosed bat is constrained by a slow life-history strategy characteristic of many tropical chiropterans. Females produce a single litter each year [F_R_i = a single litter each year], with each litter containing one or two pups [N_R_i = one or two pups]. This annual reproductive rate is modest but typical for a species that invests heavily in each offspring through extended lactation and maternal care. The timing of parturition is tightly synchronized with the peak abundance of insect prey, ensuring that the energy demands of late lactation coincide with maximal food availability. Under natural roost conditions, where ambient temperatures approximate 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C], the gestation period extends for 80 days [tg = 80 days]. This duration, which draws on comparative data from Rhinolophus ferrumequinum, is relatively protracted for a mammal of this size and likely reflects the energetic constraints imposed by the female's need to maintain both her own metabolic rate and that of the developing foetus. The synchronization of gestation length with local temperature regimes ensures that parturition occurs during the most favorable window of the year.

Sexual maturation in this species proceeds slowly relative to other small mammals, with individuals reaching puberty 365 days after birth [tp = 365 days after birth] at a temperature of 38.5 °C [T = 38.5 °C]. This critical developmental landmark is attained when the internal body temperature of the growing juvenile reaches approximately 38.5 °C [T = 38.5 °C], a thermal state indicative of full endothermic capacity. The extended period of pre-reproductive development is consistent with the bat's relatively large brain size and complex social structure, both of which require a prolonged learning phase before an individual can successfully navigate the foraging landscape and establish a position within the colony hierarchy. Young bats must acquire sophisticated echolocation skills and spatial memory of hunting routes before they can efficiently capture the large, evasive insect prey that constitutes their primary diet. The age at puberty in this population is thus a reflection of the time required to achieve both somatic maturity and ecological competence, rather than merely reaching a threshold body mass. This life-history trait places the Diadem leaf-nosed bat among the more slowly maturing members of its genus.

The maximum lifespan recorded for wild individuals of this species, measured under ambient roost conditions at 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C], is approximately 12 years [am = approximately 12 years]. This considerable longevity, equivalent to 4,380 days, is characteristic of many tropical bat species that face low extrinsic mortality from predators and have access to relatively stable food resources across their lifetime. Long-term banding studies conducted in Southeast Asian cave systems have documented individuals persisting well into their second decade, with females often remaining reproductively active for most of their adult lives. The evolution of such extended lifespans in bats is frequently linked to their ability to fly, which imposes strong selection on cellular maintenance and DNA repair mechanisms. For the Diadem leaf-nosed bat, a lifespan of this duration allows for repeated reproductive opportunities across many breeding seasons, partially offsetting the low annual fecundity of a single litter per year. This demographic strategy, combining extended longevity with low reproductive output, positions the species as a classic example of a slow life-history schedule among the Chiroptera. Continued monitoring of marked colonies will refine our understanding of age-specific survival and senescence patterns in this remarkable species.
